summary: When an emergency call reaches a Public Safety Answering Point, the device, access network and service providers may hold helpful information about the call, caller or location. This standards-track RFC describes data structures and mechanisms to convey such additional data to the PSAP.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7852 defines extra pieces of information that can travel with an emergency call, such as what kind of service the caller has, what device is calling, and who the subscriber is. Each piece is a small XML document with its own media type, so any system can recognise it. The information can be carried inside the call setup, or left on a server that the emergency centre fetches with a secure web request.

subtitle: A common set of data blocks that devices and providers can attach to an emergency call, by value or by reference.

tldr.problem: When an emergency call reaches a Public Safety Answering Point, the device, the access network and the service providers in the path all hold information about the call, the caller or the location that would help the call taker. There was no common way to pass that information along.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7852 defines five XML data blocks, each with its own MIME media type, and two ways to carry them: by value inside the SIP message body, or by reference as a URL the PSAP fetches over HTTPS. Every entity that adds data must also add a Data Provider block naming itself.
tldr.outcome: A PSAP can receive service, device and subscriber information with an emergency call and tell where each piece came from. The document is a Proposed Standard and updates RFC 6443 and RFC 6881.

today: RFC 7852 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2016. It updates RFC 6443 and RFC 6881, and it has not been obsoleted. It builds on the emergency call data work in the same series of RFCs, including RFC 4119 for location objects.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
When an IP-based emergency call is initiated, a rich set of data from multiple data sources is conveyed to the Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP). That data includes information about the calling party identity, the multimedia capabilities of the device, the request for emergency services, location information, and metadata about the sources of the data. The device, the access network provider and any service provider in the call path have even more information that is useful to a PSAP when handling an emergency.

This document extends the basic set of data communicated with an emergency call based on the Session Initiation Protocol, as described in RFC 6443 and RFC 6881, in order to carry additional data that is useful to an entity or call taker handling the call. The intent is that every emergency call carry as much of the information described here as possible.

Three categories of additional data are defined. Data associated with a location covers the primary location data conveyed in the PIDF-LO structure of RFC 4119 and its extensions for civic and geodetic location, which identifies the location or estimated location of the caller, and also secondary data specific to the location, such as floor plans, tenant and building owner contact data, and heating, ventilation and air conditioning status. That secondary data is not part of the location structure but can be transmitted using the mechanisms in this document. Data associated with a call covers the additional data known by the device making the call, the access network and service providers along the path: service provider contact information, subscriber identity and contact information, the type of service the provider and access network provide, and what type of device is being used. Data associated with a caller is personal data about a caller, such as medical information and emergency contact data. This document defines no structures in that category, but future documents can, following the procedures it sets out.

For interoperability there needs to be a common way for the information conveyed to a PSAP to be encoded and identified. Identification lets emergency services authorities know during call processing which types of data are present and whether they wish to access it, and a common encoding lets the data be successfully accessed.

Each data structure is encoded as a block of information: an XML structure with an associated MIME media type for identification within a transport such as SIP or HTTPS. The set of blocks is extensible, and registries identify the block types that may be used. Much of the information supplied by service providers and devices is private and confidential; disclosing it in the context of an emergency call is a trade-off to protect the greater interest of the customer in an emergency.
sections.plainLanguage: An emergency call already carries the caller's number and location. This document adds a place for everything else that is known along the way: the kind of line the caller has, the device model, the subscriber's details, and any provider-specific extras. It also fixes where that extra information belongs, so that a PSAP can tell what it has been sent and ignore what it cannot use.

sections.title: Document Scope
sections.content:
The scope of this document is explicitly limited to emergency calls. The data structures defined here are not appropriate to be conveyed in non-emergency calls because they carry sensitive and private data.

However, in certain private-use situations between a specialized service provider, such as a vehicle telematics service provider, and dedicated equipment, such as in a vehicle, where the endpoints have a preexisting relationship and privacy issues are addressed within that relationship, the mechanisms and data structures defined here can be used with communications within the limited context of the preexisting relationship.
sections.plainLanguage: These blocks carry personal information, so they are for emergency calls only. The one exception is a private arrangement, such as a vehicle and its tracking service, where both ends already have a relationship that handles the privacy question.

sections.title: The Five Data Blocks
sections.content:
Five data structures are defined, each as a data block with a MIME media type and an XML encoding. The Data Provider block supplies name and contact information for the entity that created the data. The Service Information block supplies information about the service. The Device Information block supplies information about the device placing the call. The Owner/Subscriber block supplies information about the owner of the device or the subscriber. The Comment block provides a way to supply free-form human-readable text to the PSAP or emergency responders; it is not intended as a general purpose extension mechanism and does not aim to provide machine-readable content.

Each block contains a mandatory DataProviderReference element, whose purpose is to associate all the blocks added by the same data provider as a unit. When a data provider adds additional data to an emergency call, such as device information, it must add information about itself through the data provider block, and the blocks it adds contain the same value in that element. All blocks added by a single entity at the same time must have the same DataProviderReference value. When the same provider processes a call more than once, likely in different roles, it adds a new set of blocks with a new value each time. The value has the same syntax and properties, specifically world-uniqueness, as the value of the Message-ID message body header field in RFC 5322, except that it is not enclosed in angle brackets.

Each block is added to the Emergency Call Additional Data registry created in Section 11.1.9, and is categorized as providing data about the caller. New blocks added to the registry in the future must also be categorized per the three categories above. The xCard format is reused in some of the data structures to provide contact information, and the document adds a new parameter value called main-number to the TYPE parameter of the tel property, since an xCard has no way to specify a main telephone number and such numbers are useful to responders called to a large enterprise.
sections.plainLanguage: There are five kinds of block. The Data Provider block is the important one: whoever sends any other block must also send this one, so the PSAP knows who the information came from. Every block carries a unique reference that groups together everything one company added to the same call.

sections.title: What Each Block Contains
sections.content:
The Data Provider block is intended to be supplied by any service provider in the path of the call, by the access network provider, and by the device. It must be supplied by any entity that provides any other block, and should be supplied by every service provider in the call path and by the access network provider if those entities add no other blocks. Its media type is application/EmergencyCallData.ProviderInfo+xml. It contains the Data Provider String, a plaintext display name; the Data Provider ID, a jurisdiction-specific code or the fully qualified domain name of the provider, which in the United States must be the NENA Company ID in the form urn:nena:companyid:<NENA Company ID> when the provider is registered with NENA; the Data Provider ID Series, which identifies the issuer of that ID and whose initial registry entries are NENA, EENA and domain; the Type of Data Provider, drawn from a registry whose initial values are Client, Access Network Provider, Telecom Provider, Telematics Provider, Language Translation Provider, Emergency Service Provider, Emergency Modality Translation, Relay Provider and Other; the Data Provider Contact URI, which should be a tel URI in E.164 format with a country code and points at a 24/7 support organization, or at the device owner when the device supplies the block; the Data Provider Language(s) Supported, a single language tag per element with the preferred language first; and an optional xCard of the data provider. Two further elements, Subcontractor Principal and Subcontractor Priority, are required when the entity providing the data is acting on behalf of another provider.

The Service Information block, with media type application/EmergencyCallData.ServiceInfo+xml, describes the service the provider gives the caller and should be included by all service providers in the path of the call. It holds the Service Environment, whose only current values are Business, Residence and Unknown; the Service Type, defining the type of service over which the call is placed, with initial values including wireless, coin, one-way, temp, MLTS-hosted, MLTS-local, sensor-unattended, sensor-attended, POTS, OTT, digital, OPX and relay; and the Service Mobility Environment, the provider's view of the mobility of the device, with values Mobile, Fixed, Nomadic and Unknown. The document is explicit that the service environment and service type are advisory: the type of service does not necessarily reflect the nature of the premises, and the registry does not cover every situation.

The Device Information block, with media type application/EmergencyCallData.DeviceInfo+xml, provides information about the device used to place the call, and should be provided by any service provider that knows what the device is and by the device itself. It holds the Device Classification, the Device Manufacturer, the Device Model Number, and a Unique Device Identifier with a TypeOfDeviceID attribute whose initial registry values are MEID, ESN, MAC, WiMAX, IMEI, IMSI, UDI, RFID and SN. It may also hold a device or service specific additional data structure, a URI that when dereferenced must yield a data structure defined by the device or service specific additional data type, and the type of that data, whose initial registry holds only IEEE1512, the United States Department of Transportation model for traffic incidents.

The Owner/Subscriber block, with media type application/EmergencyCallData.SubscriberInfo+xml, describes the owner of the device when the device provides it, or the subscriber information when a service provider provides it. The contact location is not necessarily the location of the caller or the incident but the nominal contact address. It carries a privacyRequested boolean attribute that must be provided if the block is not empty, and an xCard of the subscriber's data, which should include at least the name, organization where appropriate, address, telephone numbers and email address.
sections.plainLanguage: Each block answers a different question. The provider block says who sent the information and how to reach them. The service block says what kind of line the caller has and whether it can move. The device block says what device is calling. The subscriber block carries the contact details of the person or organisation, and a flag asking for privacy. The comment block is free text for the call taker.

sections.title: Getting New Types of Data into Use
sections.content:
Two mechanisms allow extension of the kind of data provided with an emergency call: define a new block, or define a new device or service specific additional data URL for the DeviceInfo block. While defining new data types and getting a new device or application to send the new data might be easy, getting PSAPs and responders to actually retrieve the data and use it will be difficult. New mechanism providers should understand that acquiring and using new forms of data usually requires software upgrades at the PSAP and at responders, as well as training of call takers and responders in how to interpret and use the information. Legal and operational review might also be needed. Overwhelming a call taker or responder with too much information is highly discouraged, so the barrier to supporting new data is quite high.

The mechanisms described are meant to encourage development of widely supported, common data formats for classes of devices. If all manufacturers of a class of device use the same format, and the data can be shown to improve outcomes, then PSAPs and responders can be encouraged to upgrade their systems and train their staff. Variations, however well intentioned, are unlikely to be supported. Implementors should also consider that data from sensor-based devices might not be useful to call takers or PSAPs, and that privacy, liability or other considerations might preclude the PSAP from accessing it, while still being of use to responders. Each data item provided with the call in conformance with this document can be accessed by responders or other entities in the emergency services, whether or not the PSAP accesses it.

For devices with device or service specific data there are two choices, and the data passed would likely be the same either way. Information that will be supported by many kinds of devices or services is more appropriately defined as separate blocks. Information sent as a device or service specific additional data URL in the DeviceInfo block is by reference rather than by value, which inherently provides some additional privacy protection, because the requester has to supply a certificate that the supplier verifies. Information that can be very large might be better sent in the DeviceInfo block rather than in a new block, so that implementations are unable to send it by value, while small data might best be sent in a separate block so that it can be sent by value. Providing data through the DeviceInfo block also requires a server to be available from which to retrieve it, whereas a new block can be sent by value.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding a new field is easy; getting emergency centres to use it is not. Each new kind of data needs software changes and training on the call floor, and too much information at once is worse than none. The document therefore pushes implementors towards one common format per class of device, and gives two ways to carry device-specific data, with a note on the trade-off between size, privacy and whether a server is available.

sections.title: Data Transport Mechanisms
sections.content:
Two means are specified for conveying the data to an emergency service provider. The first uses call signaling: the ability to embed a URI in the existing SIP Call-Info header field, specified in Section 20.9 of RFC 3261. The document adds a new compound token starting with the value EmergencyCallData for the Call-Info purpose parameter. When the purpose parameter starts with EmergencyCallData, the header field contains either an HTTPS URL pointing to an external resource or a Content Indirection URI that allows the data structure to be placed in the body of the SIP message. The purpose parameter also indicates the kind of data, by its MIME media subtype, that is available at the URI.

When the URI refers to data at an external resource the data is passed by reference; when it refers to data in the body of the SIP message the data is passed by value. A PSAP or emergency responder is able to examine the type of data provided and selectively access the data it is interested in, while forwarding all of it downstream. To be conveyed in a SIP body, additional data about a call is defined as a series of MIME objects, also called a block of data, each an XML data structure identified by its MIME media type, with MIME multipart enclosing them all when there is more than one. When data is passed by value, each CID URL points to one block in the body, and multiple URIs are used within a Call-Info header field, or multiple Call-Info header fields, to point to multiple blocks. When data is provided by reference, each HTTPS URL references one block and the data is retrieved with an HTTPS GET operation.

The second means embeds additional data structures in the provided-by element of a PIDF-LO. When the access network provider and the service provider are separate entities, the access network does not participate in the application-layer signaling and cannot add a Call-Info header field, but it can provide location information in a PIDF-LO from a location server, and so it can add the data structures defined in this document, or references to them, within the PIDF-LO. The data is not specific to the location itself but describes the provider's provision of it. The provided-by element is a mechanism for the access network provider to supply the information, and the document describes a namespace for inclusion in that element. The access network provider should provide additional data within a provided-by element of a PIDF-LO it returns for emergency use.

For interoperability, only blocks in the Emergency Call Additional Data registry may be sent using these mechanisms. Since multiple entities are expected to provide sets of data, the data itself needs information describing the source, so each entity adding additional data must supply a Data Provider block. All other blocks are optional, but each entity should supply all blocks where it has at least some of the information.

Failures are possible: a block might not be the type indicated by the purpose parameter, or might be badly formed. The general principle that applies to emergency calls is that it is more important for the call to go through than for everything to be correct, so most PSAPs will process a call if at all possible even if data is missing or other failures occur.

More than one Call-Info header field with a purpose value starting with EmergencyCallData can be expected, but at least one must be provided. The device must provide one unless it knows that a service provider is in the path of the call, and each service provider in the path of an emergency call must insert its own. A service provider that is unaware that the call is an emergency call and cannot reasonably be expected to determine that it is one is not expected to provide EmergencyCallData. When a block is carried in a signed or encrypted body part, the enclosing multipart has the same Content-ID as the data part, which lets an entity find the blocks it is interested in without decrypting parts it is not interested in.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two carriers. In the SIP signalling, a Call-Info header points at the data, either as a web address the PSAP fetches or as a pointer to a part of the message body. In a location object, the provided-by element does the same job, which is how an access network that never sees the SIP signalling can still contribute. Every entity that contributes data adds its own block and its own Data Provider block, and the blocks are named by media type so the PSAP can choose which to fetch.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The data structures described in this document contain information usually considered private. When information is provided by value, entities that are a party to the SIP signaling, such as proxy servers and back-to-back user agents, will have access to it and need to protect it against inappropriate disclosure, and an entity able to eavesdrop on the SIP signaling will also have access. Some Internet access types, such as in-the-clear Wi-Fi, are more vulnerable than others, such as 3G or 4G cellular data traffic, to eavesdropping. Mechanisms that protect against eavesdropping, such as TLS version 1.2 or later, should be preferentially used whenever feasible. That is not a MUST because there is an existing deployed base of clear-text SIP, and because an emergency call is more important than its protection: the call must proceed even if the TLS negotiation or certificate verification fails.

When information is provided by reference, TLS mutual authentication is required. HTTPS is required for dereferencing, the requester must use a client certificate to authenticate the HTTP request, and the provider of the information must validate the credentials provided by the requester. While a public key infrastructure with global scope might be difficult to create, the alternatives to creating devices and services that can provide critical information securely are more daunting. The provider may enforce any policy it wishes, but PSAPs and responder agencies are strongly advised to deploy a PKI so that providers of additional data can check the certificate of the requester and decide the appropriate policy based on it. TLS must be version 1.2 or later, and it is recommended to use only cipher suites that offer Perfect Forward Secrecy and avoid Cipher Block Chaining, following the recommendations in BCP 195.

Ideally the PSAP and emergency responders are given credentials signed by an authority trusted by the data provider. In most circumstances nationally recognized credentials are sufficient, because the emergency services community within a country can arrange a PKI and data providers can be provisioned with the root Certification Authority public key for the country. The data provider also needs a credential that emergency services can verify, so that they know they are receiving data from an authorized server. In the absence of such credentials, the emergency services authorities could maintain a list of local data providers' credentials obtained out of band, or obtain a credential from the DNS entry of the domain in the additional data URI, using DANE, to at least validate that the server is known to the domain providing the URI. Devices are not expected to provide data directly by reference, but rather to provide it by value or upload it to a server that can make it available and enforce security policy more easily.

Neither service providers nor devices will supply private information unless the call is recognized as an emergency call. In cellular systems such as those using 3GPP IMS, there are different procedures for placing an emergency call and a normal call. If a real emergency call is initiated as a normal call and the cellular provider recognizes this, 3GPP IMS permits the provider either to accept the call anyway or to reject it with a specific code instructing the device to retry as an emergency call. Providers ought to choose the latter, because otherwise the device will not include the information specified in this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Data sent inside the call is visible to every proxy along the way, so it should be protected with TLS where possible, and the call must still go through if the TLS handshake fails. Data sent by reference is fetched over HTTPS with a client certificate, so the server can decide who is allowed to have it. The emergency services are advised to run a public key infrastructure so that data providers can check who is asking.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
This document conveys additional information about the caller and the caller's device and service to the callee. Some of it is personal data, and privacy concerns arise. An explicit privacy indicator for information directly relating to the caller's identity is defined and its use is mandatory, but observance of the request and which information it relates to is determined by the destination jurisdiction, replicating functionality provided in some legacy emergency services systems. Data protection regulation worldwide has created exceptions for emergency services, since the drawbacks of disclosing personal data are outweighed by the benefit for the emergency caller, so the data protection rights of individuals are commonly waived for emergency situations. Some countries nevertheless offer some degree of anonymity for the caller towards PSAP call takers.

The functionality defined here far exceeds the amount of information sharing available in the legacy plain old telephone system, so additional privacy threats have to be considered. Stored data compromise is an increased risk because additional data is collected and stored in databases, and without adequate measures to secure stored data from unauthorized access at access network providers, service providers, end devices and PSAPs, individuals are exposed to potential financial, reputational or physical harm. Misattribution is a risk when the personal data collected and conveyed is incorrect or inaccurate. Identification is a risk in the sense that the calling party is identified in a much better way, and some users could feel uncomfortable with that degree of information sharing. Secondary use is a risk, because information collected for emergency services could in theory be reused for another call or for other, non-emergency purposes, and while technical measures are not in place to prevent this, policy, legal, regulatory and other non-technical approaches can be effective. Disclosure is the risk that private information is revealed when the data is not properly protected in transit or in storage.

As countermeasures, in regions where callers can elect to suppress certain personally identifying information, network or PSAP functionality can inspect privacy flags within the SIP headers to determine what information may be passed, stored or displayed, following RFC 3325, which defines the id priv-value token. The structures defined here contain privacy-sensitive data such as device identifiers, account or SIM identifiers, user contact information and the location of the caller. There is a trade-off between the privacy considerations and the utility of the data. For protection, the specification requires all retrieval of data passed by reference to be protected against eavesdropping and alteration using TLS, and security safeguards are required to prevent unauthorized access to stored data. The risks of data breaches have increased with the obligation for emergency services to retain emergency-call-related data for extended periods, several years being the norm.

The SIP communication architecture introduces further complications. When data is sent by value, all intermediaries have access to it and could introduce additional privacy risk, so where the information is privacy sensitive and intermediaries are involved, transmitting by reference might be appropriate, assuming the source of the data can operate a sufficient dereferencing infrastructure and proper access control policies are available for distinguishing the different entities dereferencing the reference. Without access control policies, any party in possession of the reference can resolve it and obtain the data, including intermediaries.
sections.plainLanguage: This data is far more than the old telephone system ever sent, and it is stored for years, so the privacy cost is real. The document offers a privacy flag the subscriber can set and urges the use of reference rather than embedded data when intermediaries are in the path, because a reference can be protected by a certificate while embedded data is readable by every proxy along the way.

viz.caption: The five data blocks and their media types

items.title: Data Provider
items.text: Name and contact information for the entity that created the data. Media type application/EmergencyCallData.ProviderInfo+xml.

items.title: Service Information
items.text: The service the caller has, whether it is a business or a residence, and how mobile it is.

items.title: Device Information
items.text: The device placing the call: classification, manufacturer, model and identifiers.

items.title: Owner/Subscriber
items.text: Details of the owner of the device or the subscriber, carried as an xCard.

items.title: Comment
items.text: Free-form human-readable text for the PSAP staff; not a general extension mechanism.
